faq.question: Why does Brent usually cost more than WTI?
faq.answer: Brent loads directly onto tankers for export while WTI must travel by pipeline from Cushing, Oklahoma to the Gulf Coast before it can reach world markets. That transport cost, plus differences in regional supply-demand balances, keeps Brent at a premium most of the time.

faq.question: What is the difference between Brent crude and WTI?
faq.answer: Brent crude originates from the North Sea and trades on ICE Futures Europe, serving as the benchmark for approximately two-thirds of global crude oil trade — particularly exports from Europe, Africa, and the Middle East. WTI (West Texas Intermediate) is a US crude benchmark traded on NYMEX with Cushing, Oklahoma as its delivery point. Brent typically trades at a slight premium to WTI due to its waterborne delivery advantage and broader international reference use.

faq.question: How does the Brent crude price affect tank terminal storage demand?
faq.answer: When the Brent crude price forward curve moves into contango — where future delivery prices exceed spot prices — storing crude becomes financially attractive, driving demand for tank terminal capacity as traders buy spot barrels and sell forward contracts to capture the price spread. In backwardation, the spot price exceeds future prices and the financial incentive to store disappears. Operators monitor the ICE Brent forward curve closely when assessing ullage demand.

faq.question: Why is Brent the international oil benchmark?
faq.answer: Brent is seaborne crude that can be shipped anywhere, so its price reflects global supply and demand rather than one region's pipeline economics. Roughly two-thirds of internationally traded crude is priced off Brent, including most Middle Eastern, African and European grades.

faq.question: How far ahead does the EIA forecast oil prices?
faq.answer: A STEO normally projects about eighteen months forward. The January edition is the exception: it extends through December of the following year, so it reaches roughly twenty-four months out. That is why the forecast horizon on this page is longest in January and shortens month by month until the next January restores it.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: Does the EIA systematically forecast oil prices too low?
faq.answer: Over the whole window the average twelve-month error is -$9.04, so on balance the projection has come in below what printed. That single figure hides more than it shows. Grouped by the year the forecast was made, the sign flips outright: 2021 vintages missed low by $35.77 at twelve months, 2024 vintages missed high by $11.61, and 2023 was the most accurate year of the record at $6.45 mean absolute error. A persistent one-directional bias is not what this shows. What it shows is a forecast that struggles at turning points, in whichever direction the turn happens to go.

faq.question: How accurate is the EIA oil price forecast?

Twelve months ahead the mean absolute error is $19.18, only 14% land within five dollars, and the average signed error is -$9.04 — meaning the forecast has on balance run below what the market delivered. faq.question: How much does the EIA revise its oil price forecast?
faq.answer: Considerably more than the confident presentation of a single number suggests. EIA’s call on the 2026 WTI average has moved across a $40.24 range over the 22 releases that have projected it: first published at $62.50 in the January 2025 edition, ranging between $47.75 and $87.99, and standing at $87.99 today. A single target month is starker still — forecasts for September 2026 ranged from $48 to $97 across successive releases before the month closed at $97.31. Reading a forecast next to its own revision path is a different experience from reading it alone, which is why both are on one page.

faq.question: How does EIA actually produce the price forecast?
faq.answer: EIA documents three inputs. A pooling model averaging five linear regressions that use futures-spot spreads, non-oil commodity prices, product crack spreads and US crude inventory changes; a separate regression on month-to-month changes in US petroleum inventories, OECD inventories relative to their four-year average, and global GDP growth; and analyst judgment, which iterates a price path against the model output, the previous month’s forecast and prevailing futures prices until the implied global balance is consistent. The last of those three is why the forecast is not simply a mechanical fu

faq.question: Which EIA series produce the price forecast?
faq.answer: Two Short-Term Energy Outlook series from Table 2, Energy Prices: WTIPUUS for the West Texas Intermediate spot average and BREPUUS for Brent, both monthly and in dollars per barrel, retrieved through EIA API v2. The realised prices every forecast is scored against are separate series from the Petroleum and Other Liquids dataset: PET.RWTC.M for Cushing WTI spot and PET.RBRTE.M for Brent.

faq.question: Why are the forecast prices whole dollars?
faq.answer: Because that is how EIA publishes them. Historical months in the same series carry cents, projected months are rounded to the nearest dollar. It is a useful reminder of the intended precision: the monthly path is a shape, not a set of point estimates accurate to the cent, and the rounding is EIA saying so.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: How is the boundary between history and forecast located?
faq.answer: STEO publishes history and projection in a single column with no flag separating them. This page finds the split by comparing the STEO series against EIA’s own published monthly spot averages and taking the newest month where the two still agree to within two cents. STEO copies the realised average into its history rows, so an observed month matches exactly and a projected month does not. The scan runs newest-first deliberately: an oldest-first walk would stop at the first restated month and wrongly treat everything after it as forecast.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: How do I tell which numbers are measured and which are projected?
faq.answer: By the line style on the chart and by the Basis column in the table. Solid lines are realised monthly spot averages; dashed lines beginning at the boundary are EIA’s projection. The two live in separate arrays in the payload rather than in one series with a marker, so a projected month cannot be drawn as history by accident. The last observed month is stated in words at the top of the page as well.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: Where does the revision history come from, if the API only serves the current forecast?
faq.answer: From EIA’s own archive. The API returns one vintage and overwrites the rest, so the earlier forecasts are read from the workbooks EIA publishes for every past release at eia.gov/outlooks/steo/archives/, which include an explicit Last Historical Month flag stating where that edition stopped reporting and started projecting. StorageCurve stores the projected months from each of those releases and adds one new vintage each month. No number in the revision history is estimated or interpolated.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: How is the error calculated?
faq.answer: Forecast minus outturn, in dollars per barrel, for every projected month that has since closed. A negative error means EIA projected a lower price than the market delivered. Mean absolute error averages the size of the miss regardless of direction; average error keeps the sign, so it shows whether the misses cancel out or lean one way. Errors are grouped by horizon, meaning the number of months between the last observed month of that release and the month being projected.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: Why does the forecast miss so badly in some years?
faq.answer: Because the errors are not spread evenly across time. They cluster around the moments when crude re-rated, and a smooth projection made months before a re-rating misses the whole of it — which is why 2021 vintages are -$35.77 at twelve months while 2023 vintages sit at $6.45 mean absolute error. That is not a peculiarity of EIA. It is the general problem with forecasting a price set by a market that has already priced in everything currently known: the large moves come from what was not known.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: What is the no-change benchmark in the error table?
faq.answer: The simplest forecast anybody can make: take the last observed monthly average and assume every future month is the same. It is included because an error figure on its own is unreadable — $19.18 at twelve months is impressive or embarrassing depending entirely on what the alternative was. On the current record the published forecast beats no-change through the first few months and then stops: from 5 months out the benchmark is the more accurate of the two ($12.72 against $13.00), and it stays ahead from there. Those rows are marked in the table above.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: What is a vintage on this page?
faq.answer: One monthly edition of the forecast, named for its first projected month. The August 2026 vintage is the release whose history stops in July 2026 and whose projection begins in August. Comparing vintages is how a revision becomes visible: the same target month, forecast repeatedly, by the same organisation, with more information each time.

Twelve months ahead the mean absolute error is $19.18, only 14% land within five dollars, and the average signed error is -$9.04 — meaning the forecast has on balance run below what the market delivered. faq.question: How far ahead does the EIA forecast oil prices?
faq.answer: A STEO normally projects about eighteen months forward. The January edition is the exception: it extends through December of the following year, so it reaches roughly twenty-four months out. That is why the forecast horizon on this page is longest in January and shortens month by month until the next January restores it.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: Does the EIA systematically forecast oil prices too low?
faq.answer: Over the whole window the average twelve-month error is -$9.04, so on balance the projection has come in below what printed. That single figure hides more than it shows. Grouped by the year the forecast was made, the sign flips outright: 2021 vintages missed low by $35.77 at twelve months, 2024 vintages missed high by $11.61, and 2023 was the most accurate year of the record at $6.45 mean absolute error. A persistent one-directional bias is not what this shows. What it shows is a forecast that struggles at turning points, in whichever direction the turn happens to go.

faq.question: How does EIA actually produce the price forecast?
faq.answer: EIA documents three inputs. A pooling model averaging five linear regressions that use futures-spot spreads, non-oil commodity prices, product crack spreads and US crude inventory changes; a separate regression on month-to-month changes in US petroleum inventories, OECD inventories relative to their four-year average, and global GDP growth; and analyst judgment, which iterates a price path against the model output, the previous month’s forecast and prevailing futures prices until the implied global balance is consistent. The last of those three is why the forecast is not simply a mechanical fu

faq.question: How much does the EIA revise its oil price forecast?
faq.answer: Considerably more than the confident presentation of a single number suggests. EIA’s call on the 2026 WTI average has moved across a $40.24 range over the 22 releases that have projected it: first published at $62.50 in the January 2025 edition, ranging between $47.75 and $87.99, and standing at $87.99 today. A single target month is starker still — forecasts for September 2026 ranged from $48 to $97 across successive releases before the month closed at $97.31. Reading a forecast next to its own revision path is a different experience from reading it alone, which is why both are on one page.

faq.question: Which EIA series produce the price forecast?
faq.answer: Two Short-Term Energy Outlook series from Table 2, Energy Prices: WTIPUUS for the West Texas Intermediate spot average and BREPUUS for Brent, both monthly and in dollars per barrel, retrieved through EIA API v2. The realised prices every forecast is scored against are separate series from the Petroleum and Other Liquids dataset: PET.RWTC.M for Cushing WTI spot and PET.RBRTE.M for Brent.

faq.question: Why are the forecast prices whole dollars?
faq.answer: Because that is how EIA publishes them. Historical months in the same series carry cents, projected months are rounded to the nearest dollar. It is a useful reminder of the intended precision: the monthly path is a shape, not a set of point estimates accurate to the cent, and the rounding is EIA saying so.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: How is the boundary between history and forecast located?
faq.answer: STEO publishes history and projection in a single column with no flag separating them. This page finds the split by comparing the STEO series against EIA’s own published monthly spot averages and taking the newest month where the two still agree to within two cents. STEO copies the realised average into its history rows, so an observed month matches exactly and a projected month does not. The scan runs newest-first deliberately: an oldest-first walk would stop at the first restated month and wrongly treat everything after it as forecast.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: Where does the revision history come from, if the API only serves the current forecast?
faq.answer: From EIA’s own archive. The API returns one vintage and overwrites the rest, so the earlier forecasts are read from the workbooks EIA publishes for every past release at eia.gov/outlooks/steo/archives/, which include an explicit Last Historical Month flag stating where that edition stopped reporting and started projecting. StorageCurve stores the projected months from each of those releases and adds one new vintage each month. No number in the revision history is estimated or interpolated.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: Why does the forecast miss so badly in some years?
faq.answer: Because the errors are not spread evenly across time. They cluster around the moments when crude re-rated, and a smooth projection made months before a re-rating misses the whole of it — which is why 2021 vintages are -$35.77 at twelve months while 2023 vintages sit at $6.45 mean absolute error. That is not a peculiarity of EIA. It is the general problem with forecasting a price set by a market that has already priced in everything currently known: the large moves come from what was not known.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: How do I tell which numbers are measured and which are projected?
faq.answer: By the line style on the chart and by the Basis column in the table. Solid lines are realised monthly spot averages; dashed lines beginning at the boundary are EIA’s projection. The two live in separate arrays in the payload rather than in one series with a marker, so a projected month cannot be drawn as history by accident. The last observed month is stated in words at the top of the page as well.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: How is the error calculated?
faq.answer: Forecast minus outturn, in dollars per barrel, for every projected month that has since closed. A negative error means EIA projected a lower price than the market delivered. Mean absolute error averages the size of the miss regardless of direction; average error keeps the sign, so it shows whether the misses cancel out or lean one way. Errors are grouped by horizon, meaning the number of months between the last observed month of that release and the month being projected.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: What is the no-change benchmark in the error table?
faq.answer: The simplest forecast anybody can make: take the last observed monthly average and assume every future month is the same. It is included because an error figure on its own is unreadable — $19.18 at twelve months is impressive or embarrassing depending entirely on what the alternative was. On the current record the published forecast beats no-change through the first few months and then stops: from 5 months out the benchmark is the more accurate of the two ($12.72 against $13.00), and it stays ahead from there. Those rows are marked in the table above.
faq.title: EIA Crude Oil Price Forecast: WTI and Brent | StorageCurve

faq.question: What is a vintage on this page?
faq.answer: One monthly edition of the forecast, named for its first projected month. The August 2026 vintage is the release whose history stops in July 2026 and whose projection begins in August. Comparing vintages is how a revision becomes visible: the same target month, forecast repeatedly, by the same organisation, with more information each time.

China has been building what analysts call the world’s largest crude oil stockpile—estimates center around roughly 1.2–1.3 billion barrels of combined strategic and commercial reserves—while continuing fresh purchases into early 2026 even as some analysts see evidence it began to use parts of that buffer during the Iran conflict [1][2][3]. Because Beijing does not publish detailed inflow/outflow figures, independent agencies and reporters reconstruct the story from import, output and refinery throughput data, creating wide but consistent consensus that China materially altered global oil balances in 2025–2026 [4][5].

The factual core is simple: China has built a very large oil buffer—around 1.2–1.3 billion barrels by most estimates—and kept adding to it into early 2026, materially changing the visible global balance [1][3][5]. The uncertainties are equally clear: exact volumes by storage type, the conditions under which Beijing would tap state versus commercial tanks, and the timing and scale of any future purchases or releases remain opaque because official disclosure is limited; public-source analysts must therefore continue to rely on indirect balance calculations that are plausible but not definitive [4][11][5].

faq.question: What is the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) in Iraq?
faq.answer:
The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also called al-Hashd al-Shaabi, is a broad coalition of Iraqi militias that came together in 2014 to fight ISIS when the Iraqi army alone was unable to prevent ISIS from taking over broad swathes of the country. The PMF took the lead in defeating ISIS along the Iraqi front. As a result of its success, the Iraqi government formally recognized it as an auxiliary to the armed forces, granting legitimacy to the coalition and salaries to its fighters.

The PMF includes militias from several different political orientations, including Iran-backed Shiʿi militias, Shiʿi militias that oppose Iranian intervention in Iraq, and militias that represent Sunni, Christian, and Yazidi communities. The predominant militias are Iranian-backed members of the Axis of Resistance, including Kataeb Hezbollah, the Badr Organization, ʿAṣāʾib Ahl al-Ḥaqq, and oppose U.S. intervention in Iraq.

Despite the PMF’s status as an auxiliary to the armed forces, it was not fully integrated and some of the constituent militias continue to operate independently of the state, including attacking U.S. forces during periods of tension. Under pressure from the United States in 2026, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the militias to come under direct state authority.

Throughout 2026 the Strait of Hormuz remained a core flash‑point of the U.S.–Iran confrontation; the waterway was effectively closed to commercial shipping from early March 2026 and intermittent Iranian attacks on, and threats to, vessels continued through at least October 2026, demonstrating that geopolitical tensions endured well into the latter half of the year.
* The strait was “effectively closed” to commercial traffic from 2 Mar 2026 (U.S.‑Israeli strikes) and remained largely non‑operational for the rest of the year.

* Iranian forces conducted periodic attacks on commercial shipping and issued repeated threats to close or restrict passages (e.g., Oct 7 2026 Iranian adviser’s statement; Oct 14 2026 live‑tracker showing only 2 ships transiting vs. a normal ~85 /day).

* A short‑lived cease‑fire agreed in mid‑June 2026 collapsed by early July, and a subsequent “memorandum of understanding” intended to end the conflict by 30 June 2026 had “become virtually defunct” after Iran struck three commercial vessels in July 2026.
* International bodies (IMO, ICC, World Economic Forum) reported sustained disruption to global energy and food supply chains through the remainder of 2026.

The persisting tensions matter because the Strait handles roughly **30 % of world seaborne‑traded crude oil** and a substantial share of global liquefied natural gas. Continued closures or restrictions:
* Drive up maritime insurance war‑risk premiums (reported 30 × pre‑crisis rates).
* Cause acute supply‑chain shocks for oil‑dependent economies, fertilizer raw‑material shipments, and food‑price stability (ICC warned of +80 % grain‑price spikes if restrictions continued).
* Influence global oil‑price volatility (Brent fell from a peak of $118 in March 2026 to $71 by July, but rebounded as tensions re‑escalated).
* Affect geopolitical stability in the Gulf, prompting regional powers (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar) to seek alternative routes or diplomatic de‑escalation.

faq.question: What is the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) in Iraq?
faq.answer:
The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also called al-Hashd al-Shaabi, is a broad coalition of Iraqi militias that came together in 2014 to fight ISIS when the Iraqi army alone was unable to prevent ISIS from taking over broad swathes of the country. The PMF took the lead in defeating ISIS along the Iraqi front. As a result of its success, the Iraqi government formally recognized it as an auxiliary to the armed forces, granting legitimacy to the coalition and salaries to its fighters.

The PMF includes militias from several different political orientations, including Iran-backed Shiʿi militias, Shiʿi militias that oppose Iranian intervention in Iraq, and militias that represent Sunni, Christian, and Yazidi communities. The predominant militias are Iranian-backed members of the Axis of Resistance, including Kataeb Hezbollah, the Badr Organization, ʿAṣāʾib Ahl al-Ḥaqq, and oppose U.S. intervention in Iraq.

Despite the PMF’s status as an auxiliary to the armed forces, it was not fully integrated and some of the constituent militias continue to operate independently of the state, including attacking U.S. forces during periods of tension. Under pressure from the United States in 2026, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the militias to come under direct state authority.

faq.question: Why are European refinery margins higher than US margins?
faq.answer: Europe imports 80%+ crude (mostly Russia pre-2022). At supply disruptions there (sanctions, crises) local refiners command premiums because alternatives vanish. The US has domestic oil (Shale), diversified imports, more refinery capacity per capita. So margins are less volatile.

faq.question: What's the difference between crack spread and refining margin?

faq.question: Is there a limit to how high refining margins can go?

Long-term, margins stabilize when new refinery capacity comes online (takes 5–10 years to build).

text: # Research Record: China Filling Strategic Reserves at 1.0 Million b/d Pace

The observation that China is filling strategic reserves at approximately 1.0 million barrels per day is **supported by official U.S. EIA data**, which estimates China added an average of **1.1 million barrels per day** to its strategic oil inventories throughout 2025, reaching nearly 1.4 billion barrels by year-end. The 1.0 million b/d figure falls within the range of estimates from independent analysts (900,000–1.1 million bpd), though the exact pace varies by methodology and time window. China does not publicly disclose its reserve levels, so all figures are derived from import, export, refining, and third-party inventory data.

Research establishes that China significantly increased its strategic oil inventories during 2025, with the best‑available estimate being an average addition of ~1.1 million barrels per day according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA, April 2026). This accumulation contributed to China ending 2025 with nearly 1.4 billion barrels of strategic reserves—more than three times the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) level of 413 million barrels. The 1.0 million b/d observation is consistent with the EIA’s central estimate and with several independent analyses, though some methodologies (e.g., S&P Global Commodity Insight’s year‑to‑date estimate of 530,000 bpd) yield lower figures.
(Multiple EIA‑derived results consistently report the 1.1 million bpd figure.)
(Note: This is a year‑to‑date snapshot, not the full‑year average.)

- **China does not officially report reserve data.** All figures are estimates derived from trade, production, and refinery data, with methodologies varying between government‑held SPR, commercial stockpiles, and “strategic‑plus‑commercial” aggregates.

- China’s reserve buildup was partly enabled by relatively low oil prices during much of 2025, allowing opportunistic purchasing. The government directed state‑owned oil companies to stockpile as part of its energy‑security strategy, especially after the Russia‑Ukraine war highlighted import‑dependency risks.

results.title: IEA warns diesel supply crunch to last into 2027
results.description: The International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday that global diesel and gasoil markets will remain under significant strain well into 2027, with the replenishment of depleted inventories unlikely before the second half of next year.
extraSnippets: The International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday that global diesel and gasoil markets will remain under significant strain well into 2027, with the replenishment of depleted inventories unlikely before the second half of next year. According to the IEA's October Oil Market Report, Singapore diesel prices climbed above $200 a barrel in mid-September, while Europe and the United States saw record highs of roughly $220 a barrel.

According to IEA data, September global diesel exports were 700,000 barrels a day below year-earlier levels, as a 1.3 million barrel-per-day shortfall from Russia and the Middle East swamped incremental gains from other suppliers. Even with a recovery in refinery throughputs expected toward year-end, gasoil supply falls short of meeting demand in the fourth quarter, the IEA said. Higher global refinery output will return the gasoil market to a surplus in the first quarter of 2027, but that will be insufficient to offset the deficit built up during 2026.

The IEA said the market balance remains dependent on a recovery of product supply from the Middle East, and that failing such a recovery, further demand reductions may be needed to balance markets. The IEA observed that "relatively price inelastic diesel demand has remained strong," buoyed in part by government programs designed to shield consumers from high fuel costs. Diesel will account for 25% of the 2.6 million barrel-per-day annual decline in global oil demand the agency forecast for 2026.

Record diesel prices are already raising the cost of goods and weighing on real incomes, economic activity, and inflation, the IEA said. The warning comes after President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel into global markets, beginning with 300,000 metric tons immediately, in a bid to address elevated fuel prices ahead of November midterm elections.

record.finding: Major oil companies shifting capital from traditional crude expansion to LNG projects
record.importance: Strategic capital reallocation by major oil companies from crude expansion toward LNG projects in 2024-2025
record.evidence: Six major integrated oil companies (ExxonMobil, Chevron, Shell, BP, Equinor, TotalEnergies) are expected to ease combined capital expenditures to about $110.2 billion in 2026 from $114.1 billion in 2025, shifting focus from broad expansion to high-return upstream and LNG projects. Combined capital expenditures of six major oil companies totaled $109.5-116.5 billion in 2024 compared with $113.3 billion in 2023. TotalEnergies' capital expenditures reached $17.1 billion in 2025 with around one-third devoted to new oil and gas projects. ExxonMobil anticipates total annual capital expenditures and exploration expenses of $23-25 billion in 2024 and $22-27 billion annually from 2025 through 2027. Advantaged assets in the Permian, Guyana, and LNG represented 59% of production in 2025, an increase of approximately 7 percentage points from 2024. TotalEnergies plans capital spending of about $15 billion in 2026.
